sources.title: Bonnie J. McCay and Joan Bennett, "Elinor Ostrom 1933-2012" -- National Academy of Sciences Biographical Memoir (2014)

persistence.rationale: The NAS memoir documents a poor-background childhood and a gap of roughly a decade between her 1954 undergraduate degree and 1965 doctorate, spent partly in non-academic employee-relations and personnel roles (corroborated by the encyclopedia entry's specific job titles and dates) before she was able to return to graduate study and an eventual professorship.

risk_tolerance.rationale: Documented 2010 interview quote (cited in the NAS memoir) describing her deliberate choice to zero out her own salary at points to support junior faculty -- a specific, dated act of accepting real personal financial cost for a stated institutional-building goal.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: Documented real, dated 1954 gender discrimination in the academic job market described in the NAS memoir as a direct contributor to her decade-long detour into non-academic employee-relations work before returning to a doctorate -- a specific, sourced adverse incident, not an assumed hardship.

resourcefulness.rationale: Inferred from her documented sequence of employee-relations and personnel-department roles (Godfrey L. Cabot Inc., then UCLA) that she leveraged into eventual re-entry to academia, though neither source documents the specific mechanism of that transition.

achievement_drive.rationale: Documented steady rise from visiting assistant professor in 1965 to the endowed Arthur F. Bentley Professor of Political Science by 1991, and eventual sole-woman 2009 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for pioneering common-pool-resource research -- an independently verifiable institutional and scholarly record.

collaboration.rationale: Inferred from her documented simultaneous co-directorship of the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis and the Center for the Study of Institutions, Population, and Environmental Change -- both explicitly collaborative, co-led research centers, though the sources describe the roles more than specific collaborative incidents.

curiosity.rationale: Inferred from her documented research spanning cognitive science, institutional economics, and environmental policy, though neither source gives a dated curiosity-specific incident.

impact_motivation.rationale: Documented sustained focus across her career on how real institutions govern shared common-pool resources (fisheries, forests, irrigation systems) rather than abstract theory alone, and the concrete salary-zeroing act above, both pointing toward a documented orientation to material outcomes for others.

holdReason: Validator output (mechanical, not adjusted): 8 scored attributes against the 18-attribute floor, 0.245 coverage against 0.6, only 1 attribute at confidence>=0.5 against the 12-attribute floor. This is the thinnest of the eight roster-18 candidates -- the two sources actually consulted (NAS memoir, Encyclopedia.com) document career/institutional history and two genuine incidents (1954 job-market discrimination, deliberate salary sacrifice) well, but not enough dated behavioral specificity across the thinking/creativity/work_style facets to score defensibly. Held, not rescued: no attempt was made to inflate confidence or add rows without new evidence to cross the floor.

provenance.notes: Roster-18 intake (2026-09), stricter multi-source gate. Wikidata identity (Q153761) checked against the live Wikipedia article before scoring. Both sources actually fetched and read in full: the NAS Biographical Memoir (McCay & Bennett, 2014) via direct PDF fetch, the Encyclopedia.com entry via direct page fetch. A candidate second source specifically identified in the NAS memoir's own references (an Annual Reviews 'Conversations' interview transcript with Margaret Levi) was attempted but returned a dead link (404) -- not substituted with a weaker source merely to pad the count; the two sources actually read are reported honestly. This is the thinnest evidence base of the eight roster-18 candidates: real incidents exist (1954 discrimination, deliberate salary sacrifice) but the two sources consulted describe career/institutional history more than dated behavioral incidents, which caps confident scoring at a moderate number of attributes.
